title: The Influence Operation That Ran on Borrowed Reputations | Council on Foreign Relations
gist: OpenAI exposed a Russian influence operation that used ChatGPT to build a fake Israel-based 'expert institute' (IBI) complete with fabricated affiliates, plagiarized research, and a pro-Russia 'sovereignty index,' then generated multilingual social posts across X, LinkedIn, Facebook, Substack, and Telegram — illustrating how AI now lets influence actors build credible-looking institutional infrastructure at low cost, even though this particular campaign's actual reach stayed modest.

themes.theme: Anatomy of an AI-enabled influence operation

insights.claim: The International Burke Institute (IBI) presents itself as an Israel-based expert community with research papers, a proprietary sovereignty index, and a roster of affiliates including at least three current or former CFR experts — none of whom had ever heard of IBI — with much of its academic content appearing copied and misattributed.
insights.speaker: Jessica Brandt
insights.so_what: Fabricated think tanks falsely listing real experts as affiliates is a reputational-hijacking tactic that any named expert or institution should actively monitor for and correct, since victims may not discover the misuse until it's flagged externally.

insights.claim: OpenAI disclosed that Russian influence actors used VPNs to log into ChatGPT and generate mostly-English social media posts that later appeared across X, LinkedIn, Facebook, Substack, and Telegram, with actors explicitly instructing ChatGPT to hide linguistic clues that would reveal their Russian origin.
insights.speaker: Jessica Brandt
insights.so_what: Explicit prompting to strip linguistic 'tells' shows influence operators are actively using AI to defeat traditional detection heuristics (language-mistake patterns) that previously helped identify foreign campaigns.

insights.claim: The posts criticized Ukraine, the European Union, and other Western governments while advocating better relations with Russia, and heavily promoted IBI and its sovereignty index, which itself praises Russia and denigrates the West — a two-layer structure where fabricated 'independent' analysis launders the same message the raw social posts pushed directly.
insights.speaker: Jessica Brandt
insights.so_what: This dual-layer laundering (fake institute + social amplification) is a template to watch for in other influence campaigns — a credible-looking 'expert' source citation makes propaganda far more persuasive than raw social posts alone.

insights.claim: IBI disputed reporting by Le Monde on the OpenAI report but did not address that UNICEF denied being an IBI partner institution despite IBI's website still claiming that partnership; the organization lists no founder or leader, and its unsigned pushback statement came from an entity that continues posting content on a still-live website.
insights.speaker: Jessica Brandt
insights.so_what: A fabricated UNICEF partnership claim that IBI has not corrected, combined with total anonymity of leadership, is a concrete, checkable red flag pattern for identifying other astroturfed 'institutes.'

themes.theme: Scale of the operation: modest reach, substantial infrastructure

insights.claim: This influence operation's actual reach was modest — most posts did not receive substantial views, and OpenAI placed it at the low end of level three of the six-level Breakout Scale (multiple platforms reached, with some indications of breakout to authentic audiences) — yet the effort's creation of a full fake-institution infrastructure with purported expert affiliates, research papers, and a proprietary index is what stands out as notable.
insights.speaker: Jessica Brandt
insights.so_what: Low measured reach does not mean low risk — the infrastructure-building capability (fake institutes, personas, fabricated papers) is the reusable, scalable asset, and its low cost via AI tools means future iterations could achieve much larger reach with the same techniques.

insights.claim: Operators used AI-generated personas, profile photos, and face-to-camera video reels, and attempted to seed fabricated research papers with fictitious authors on authentic academic research-hosting platforms — activity Meta disrupted on Facebook and Instagram after reviewing information OpenAI shared.
insights.speaker: Jessica Brandt
insights.so_what: AI-generated video personas and fabricated academic papers targeting legitimate research platforms represent an escalation in influence-operation sophistication that traditional bot-detection methods (built around text/image patterns) may not catch.

insights.claim: Russia has long attempted to launder campaigns across multiple platforms and manufacture credibility by disguising content as authentic domestic voices; this campaign's cross-platform, hidden-hand approach is emblematic of a maturation of influence operations over the past decade that AI is now accelerating rather than fundamentally inventing.
insights.speaker: Jessica Brandt
insights.so_what: AI should be understood as an accelerant of existing, well-documented Russian influence tradecraft rather than a wholly new threat category — useful framing for calibrating policy responses toward scaling existing detection capacity rather than building entirely new frameworks.
insights.quote: accelerating, if not wholly revolutionizing, foreign information operations

themes.theme: Policy implication: institutionalize AI-lab threat reporting

insights.claim: The episode highlights the value of regular threat intelligence reporting from AI labs, which have unique insight into consequential activity that social media platforms and governments may not see, and the author argues AI labs should routinize such reporting the way social media companies have done over the past decade.
insights.speaker: Jessica Brandt
insights.so_what: Institutionalized AI-lab threat reporting would create a public-interest record enabling investigative research and cross-company action — a policy ask that, if adopted, could become a new standard disclosure practice worth tracking across major AI labs (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google).
